title: Is the Common Core all about Technology?
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. takes aim at the habit of equating Common Core alignment with putting devices in classrooms, prompted by an educator who described his district's alignment effort as giving every elementary classroom iPads. He audits the CCSS ELA/Literacy anchor standards and finds only three that explicitly mention digital technology and three more that reasonably imply it. From that audit he argues that most of the standards can be taught without technology, because they center on old-school literacies, and that this matters for equal access to a quality education regardless of school budgets. He contends that true 21st-century skills are the same as 20th-century ones: reading, writing, thinking, speaking, and (outside the standards) character. He offers his own schooling as a case study, noting that he learned new platforms easily as they appeared because his foundation was literacy instruction and character mentoring rather than classroom tech. The piece closes by conceding a place for teaching technology while insisting that the bulk of instructional time belongs to core literacies that require little more than a book, pen and paper.
points: Stuart's count of the CCSS ELA/Literacy anchor standards finds only three (W.CCR.6, W.CCR.9, SL.CCR.5) that explicitly reference digital technology, with three more that merely imply it.
He frames the no-tech-needed reading of the standards as an equity argument: schools without device budgets can still teach most of the CCSS well.
His list of durable skills (reading, writing, thinking, speaking, and being a person of character) is offered as the real content of "21st century skills."
Using his own story, he argues that students with strong literacy foundations pick up new platforms such as Facebook, blogs and search on their own as they arrive.

The practical upshot is a time-allocation claim: most instructional time should go to core literacies, since polished tech products are worthless if students cannot really read, write, think and speak.
quotes: This kind of thinking isn't unique. I frequently see the CCSS being synonymized with classroom tech. This got me wondering: how much of the actual CCSS ELA/Literacy standards explicitly mention technology?

Nothing has changed here: technology can be incorporated into learning just about any skill, and that probably includes all of those mentioned in the CCSS. But, to me, this begs a question: do you need technology to teach most of the CCSS?

For the sake of increasing equal access to a quality education regardless of school budgets, I would argue that, no, you do not need technology to teach most of the CCSS because the CCSS focuses on core, old school literacies.

Yet, when Facebook came out, I figured out how to use it. When blogs became accessible via Blogger and WordPress, I figured them out. I figured out how to Google and how to determine the strengths and weaknesses of a given source on the Internet.

To what do I credit my success? I certainly lack an outstanding innate talent or intelligence. Rather, I thank God for a boatload of reading, writing, thinking, and speaking instruction, and key character mentors who essentially taught me to work hard and be nice.

As a member of the high school graduating class of 2002 and the college graduating class of 2006, the snazziest technology I could access in elementary school was the occasional game of Frogger on a classroom Macintosh. By the time I graduated high school, Hotmail was just coming into vogue, AOL Instant Messenger was the coolest thing I could do on my home's dial-up Internet connection, and the term “Web 2.0” was still a nerd-only word.
